identification.summary: IndigoZebra is a suspected Chinese-speaking cyber-espionage group that has targeted Central Asian governments since at least 2014 [S1][S8]. Kaspersky first named it in its Q2 2017 APT Trends report, describing activity against former Soviet republics using Meterpreter, Poison Ivy, xDown and a previously unknown backdoor it called xCaon [S6][S5]. In July 2021 Check Point Research reported a spear-phishing campaign against the Afghan National Security Council that delivered BoxCaon, a new xCaon variant that uses Dropbox for command and control [S1][S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Activity since at least 2014: Check Point found about 30 xCaon samples, the earliest from 2014 [S1][S4]. First public naming was Kaspersky's Q2 2017 APT Trends report (dated 2017-08-08 per Malpedia) [S6][S7].
identification.notes: No Microsoft name for IndigoZebra was found in the searches run for this record (Microsoft's naming mapping could not be opened); the encyclopedia keeps the vendor name IndigoZebra. MITRE tracks the group as G0136 [S8]. Check Point described the 2021 Afghan activity as only 'believed' to be IndigoZebra, based on malware links to the earlier xCaon cluster [S2][S4].

attribution.sponsor: Suspected China-linked. Kaspersky listed IndigoZebra among Chinese-speaking actors [S5][S6], and Check Point called it a Chinese-speaking group [S2]. Check Point named no government sponsor [S2][S4].
attribution.confidence: Vendor assessment only. Kaspersky made no definitive attribution in 2017 [S5]. Check Point's language is 'Chinese-speaking' and 'believed to be' IndigoZebra [S2][S4]. Malpedia's 'Chinese state-sponsored' label is stronger than the primary vendors' wording [S7]. No government attribution was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Malware lineage (xCaon to BoxCaon) and code overlap linking the 2021 Afghan intrusions to earlier Central Asian activity [S1][S4]. Kaspersky noted ties to other Chinese-speaking actors in 2017 [S5].

objectives: Political and government espionage against Central Asian states, including Afghanistan's National Security Council and political entities in Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan [S1][S3][S4].

targeting.notes: Check Point telemetry showed the HTTP-based xCaon variants mainly targeted political entities in Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan [S3]. Check Point said the campaign may extend beyond the three named countries; these were the ones it could confidently tie to the victim list [S2].

capabilities.summary: Kaspersky's 2017 report described a toolset of Meterpreter, Poison Ivy, xDown and the custom xCaon backdoor [S5][S6]. The xCaon family (about 30 samples since 2014) used HTTP for C2 [S1]. BoxCaon, the 2021 variant, uses an attacker-controlled Dropbox account as C2. It creates a unique folder per victim, reads commands from a sub-folder named 'd', and writes results back to Dropbox, so its traffic blends with legitimate HTTPS cloud-storage use [S1][S5]. BoxCaon's features are narrow: file download and upload, command execution, and returning results. That is enough to stage further reconnaissance and lateral-movement tools [S1]. Initial access in 2021 was by spear-phishing that impersonated the Administrative Office of the President of Afghanistan, with a password-protected RAR archive leading to a backdoor dropped as 'spools.exe' [S3][S4]. MITRE lists Poison Ivy, xCaon and BoxCaon as associated software [S8].

campaigns.name: Early xCaon activity in Central Asia
campaigns.summary: The earliest xCaon samples date from 2014. HTTP variants mainly targeted political entities in Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan.

campaigns.name: Kaspersky APT Trends Q2 2017 disclosure
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky first named IndigoZebra. It described activity against former Soviet republics using Meterpreter, Poison Ivy, xDown and the new xCaon backdoor, and listed the group among Chinese-speaking actors.

campaigns.name: Afghan National Security Council spear-phishing
campaigns.summary: NSC officials received lure emails claiming to come from the Administrative Office of the President of Afghanistan. They carried a password-protected RAR archive that installed a backdoor.

campaigns.name: Check Point BoxCaon report
campaigns.summary: Check Point Research published its analysis of BoxCaon (Dropbox C2) and linked the Afghan intrusions to the long-running IndigoZebra activity against Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan.

diamond.adversary: Suspected Chinese-speaking espionage operators; government sponsorship not confirmed by the reporting vendors [S2][S4][S5].
diamond.capability: Spear-phishing with government-impersonation lures and password-protected RAR archives; custom xCaon/BoxCaon backdoors; commodity Poison Ivy, Meterpreter and xDown [S1][S3][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: HTTP C2 for older xCaon variants; attacker-controlled Dropbox account with a per-victim folder structure for BoxCaon [S1][S5].
diamond.victim: Afghan National Security Council; government and political entities in Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan; former Soviet republics more broadly [S1][S2][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection on Central Asian governments [S1][S4].
diamond.technology: Abuse of trusted cloud storage (Dropbox) as C2, and trust in inter-agency email from senior government offices [S1][S3].

gaps: The Check Point Research report, Check Point blog, Kaspersky Securelist report and MITRE page could not be fetched in this session (network errors). Facts are drawn from search-result excerpts and secondary coverage of those documents and should be verified against the originals.
No Microsoft name was confirmed; Microsoft's MicrosoftMapping.json could not be accessed.
No public reporting after 2021 was found; current activity status is unknown.
No government attribution or indictment was found. Malpedia's 'state-sponsored' label goes beyond what Kaspersky and Check Point state.
Whether the 2021 intrusions succeeded in exfiltrating data, and the full victim set beyond Afghanistan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, are not public in the sources gathered.
Specific IOCs (Dropbox tokens, domains, hashes) were not retrieved; secondary claims about a hardcoded bearer token were not verified against Check Point.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Relevant terrain is the email and cloud-storage traffic of Central Asian partner governments' national security and presidential offices, plus coalition personnel who exchange mail with them [S1][S4]. STEP 2: Allowed cloud-storage services (Dropbox) give the actor C2 that blends into normal HTTPS. Long-running custom tooling since 2014 shows patience and persistence [S1]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is a spear-phish impersonating a senior government office, then a password-protected RAR, then the xCaon/BoxCaon backdoor, then Dropbox-based tasking, then follow-on reconnaissance tools [S1][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued collection on Central Asian government policy and security deliberations through impersonation phishing. MDCOA is use of a compromised partner-government mailbox to phish US or coalition personnel working regional security issues, giving access to shared planning data; this is an extrapolation, not observed. Candidate indicators: password-protected RAR attachments claiming senior-office origin, endpoints making Dropbox API calls with no sanctioned Dropbox use, and a new 'spools.exe' or similar look-alike system binary [S1][S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: flag Dropbox and other cloud-storage API traffic from mission and partner-liaison enclaves, because BoxCaon C2 resembles legitimate use [S1]. (2) Authorities: activity is vendor-attributed only, so treat it as a suspected PRC-linked espionage threat and avoid overstating government attribution in products [S2][S4]. (3) Mission assurance: harden email trust paths with Central Asian partner governments, since lures impersonated a presidential office [S3]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with partner-nation CERTs in Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and the region, and with commercial vendors, because public reporting has been sparse since 2021.

provenance.importedSummary: IndigoZebra is a Chinese state-sponsored actor mentioned for the first time by Kaspersky in its APT Trends report Q2 2017, targeting, at the time of its discovery, former Soviet Republics with multiple malware strains including Meterpreter, Poison Ivy, xDown, and a previously unknown backdoor called “xCaon.”
